one_line: provider OHLC input validation is INCONSISTENT and individually-INCOMPLETE across all three implementors: (1) PolygonProvider.fetchDaily maps r.o/r.h/r.l/r.c with NO finite/positive guard at all; (2) AlphaVantage parseFiniteOrNull guards non-finite but lets a literal 0/negative through (Number.isFinite(0)===true) — its doc-comment misleadingly claims it stops 0-price injection, which it does NOT (it only stops missing->0 coercion); (3) Yahoo skips close==null||close<=0 but a NaN close slips (NaN<=0 is false). DISPOSITION (owner, A5-DORMANCY-shaped but lean COMPLETE not delete — the Report-Only->enforce plan shows intent to ship strict CSP): finish the nonce path (consume x-nonce in the root layout to nonce Next's scripts, and/or set the nonce'd CSP on the REQUEST headers) OR remove the dead nonce scaffolding if abandoning strict CSP. one_line: A workflow-level permissions block is a CEILING, not a default: refresh-data.yml declared contents:write at workflow level while its alert job requested issues:write, so GitHub rejected the ENTIRE FILE - startup_failure with zero jobs - and the weekly refresh was dead on main for the THIRD time in this package
citation: Verified live on workflow_dispatch run 33646555241 (2026-09-02): 'This run likely failed because of a workflow file issue', jobs total_count=0. nightly-backtest and stryker-weekly declare no workflow-level block and were unaffected
status: FIXED 2026-09-02. issues:write added to the ceiling and a test asserts every scope an alert job requests is within its workflow's ceiling, with the extractors themselves asserted non-vacuous. THE LESSON: the previous test checked the alert job HAD the permission. It did. What was never checked is whether the workflow PERMITTED it to take effect - presence without reachability, in the package written about reachability. And startup_failure reads identically to the unparseable-workflow break this same package shipped a week earlier, so the symptom is not diagnostic; read the run's own message.

one_line: The SAME permission-ceiling rule one level down: a caller job's permissions block is the ceiling for the reusable workflow it invokes, and all three callers granted only issues:write while the called job asks for contents:read to run actions/checkout - so GitHub rejected EVERY wired workflow with startup_failure, zero jobs
citation: nightly-backtest succeeded on bece0c7 and 9dd300b then startup_failure from 4396ba0 onward, and it has NO workflow-level permissions block - which is what proved Q107-A20 (the workflow-level ceiling) was a real defect but NOT the cause of this symptom. refresh-data dispatch runs 33646555241 and 33947912680 both startup_failure
status: FIXED 2026-09-05. contents:read added to the caller grant in all three wired workflows, and a test asserts every scope the CALLED workflow asks for is granted by each caller, with both extractors asserted non-vacuous. Watched it fail by reverting one caller; green on revert. THREE LESSONS: (1) the ceiling rule applies at BOTH hops and checking one hop of a two-hop chain is not checking the chain; (2) the contents:read that broke this was added to FIX a red-team finding about checkout needing it - a correct fix, incomplete at the other end; (3) I mis-attributed the symptom in Q107-A20, finding A problem and assuming it was THE problem. startup_failure has now had three distinct causes in this package and remains non-diagnostic.

one_line: nightly-backtest ran startup_failure on 2026-09-03 and 2026-09-04 and NOTHING notified anyone - because the notification mechanism is precisely what was broken; a self-referential blind spot where the alerting cannot report its own failure to start
citation: Runs on 4396ba0 both startup_failure; no issue was opened; discovered only by manually listing run history during an unrelated inspection
status: OPEN 2026-09-05. Q107-A21 fixes the immediate cause, but the STRUCTURAL gap remains: an alert that lives inside the workflow it watches cannot fire when the workflow fails to start. A startup_failure produces zero jobs, so no job of any kind runs. Closing this needs an out-of-band check - a separate workflow, or a scheduled probe that asserts each watched workflow has a completed run within its expected cadence. Until then, treat 'no alert' as 'no information', not as 'healthy'.

one_line: ROOT CAUSE of four consecutive rejected workflow files: validation used yaml.safe_load() plus regexes over the file text - a PROXY whose leniency differs from the consumer's. PyYAML accepts a duplicate mapping key (last wins) while GitHub Actions rejects the file outright, so a checker more permissive than the thing it stands in for produces false negatives by construction
citation: Measured: actionlint 1.7.12 pinpoints the nested-expression bug at refresh-data.yml:178:19 and a DUPLICATED env key at :85:9. The duplicate was introduced by the Q107-A23 fix itself and reached a pull request with every local check green; actionlint found it before merge. It does NOT catch the two permission-ceiling bugs, which the custom tests cover
status: FIXED 2026-09-05. npm run lint:workflows (pinned actionlint, fails loudly if the binary cannot install, refuses to report success on an empty file set) folded into check:ci and added as a CI job. Division of labour measured rather than assumed: actionlint catches BUG-1 (nested expression) and BUG-4 (duplicate key); the architecture tests catch BUG-2 and BUG-3 (workflow-level and caller->callee permission ceilings), which actionlint does not model. THE GENERAL LESSON: when a domain has a real validator, use it - a bespoke checker only ever knows the bugs you have already found, and a green result from a more permissive proxy is not evidence.

Regression test uses an INDEPENDENT ORACLE over all 56 fixtures plus a one-directional property, not pinned constants. Watched it fail against the original; green on revert. WORST BUG OF THE WAVE: crash-in-2022-recover-by-2026 is the MODAL shape for this universe, so the platform systematically told users risk was lower than it was.

The property test with an independent oracle is what should have caught this, and now exists.

The reset is correct and kept, but it is LATENT, not live: Next.js App Router keys each dynamic route segment by its VALUE, so navigating /stock/AAPL -> /stock/MSFT UNMOUNTS and REMOUNTS the page component and every hook inside it. Reproduced identically on localhost dev for both /stock/[ticker] and /sector/[slug]. Both call sites (stock page, sector page) pass a ticker that CANNOT change without a remount, so the missing reset was never reachable from the UI. Keep the fix - the hook is a reusable API and the sibling useLiveQuotes DOES have a caller (app/page.tsx:110) whose ticker LIST changes in place - but the earlier claim that users saw the previous security's price under the new ticker's name is WITHDRAWN. one_line: The I2 cache guard defined its producer set as files.filter(f => /_cached:\s*true/) - 'routes that already set the flag' - so a route that serves a stored copy WITHOUT the flag was not a producer, and the exact violation the guard exists to catch was the one input it could not see. CLAUDE.md's claim that this clause was CLOSED by Q-101 was FALSE
citation: Measured 2026-09-05 with a structural detector: SIX routes return a module-level stored value; three set the flag (chart/[ticker], crypto/btc/metrics, crypto/btc/liquidations) and three did NOT - app/api/ma-deviation (5-min TTL), app/api/backtest (ONE HOUR) and app/api/backtest/live (60s). All 24 assertions in the guard were green throughout. Verified live against the dev server: two successive GETs of /api/ma-deviation returned _cached false then true with an identical _cachedAt
status: FIXED 2026-09-05. __tests__/architecture/cacheSubstitution.ts detects the substitution structurally (module-level mutable store, written, then referenced inside a NextResponse.json argument - directly, via spread, or via a local bound to it). The three silent routes now emit _cached AND _cachedAt, and each has a DataFreshnessIndicator consumer; at a one-hour TTL a boolean says 'a cache was involved' where the user needs 'how old'. Watched it fail on the committed tree: it named all three, and reintroducing the detector's own historical spread bug fails four tests. SIXTH SHAPE of the guard-reachability defect and the first where the SET was defined by the property under test: a filter written in terms of the answer cannot find a counterexample. Named residuals asserted as passing tests - a store read through an unmodelled expression, a store served from the second argument onward, a cache living in a shared lib/ helper.

one_line: NAMED RESIDUAL of Q110-P2: the _cached BOOLEAN is defeated by any cache ABOVE the code that sets it. These routes send Cache-Control max-age, so a browser or CDN can answer from its own store with a body whose _cached was frozen as false when first computed - a stored copy served as live, which is the exact substitution I2 forbids, one layer up
citation: MEASURED in the browser 2026-09-05: two DEFAULT fetches of /api/ma-deviation returned _cached:false with an IDENTICAL _cachedAt (proving the second never reached the server), while the same pair with cache:'no-store' returned _cached:true. The badge showed 'Data: ~34s ago' when it should have shown Cached. The _cachedAt TIMESTAMP does not have this failure mode - an age is recomputed from the clock on every render, so it keeps climbing even inside a stale body
status: PARTIALLY FIXED 2026-09-05. app/ma-deviation/page.tsx now fetches no-store, matching the two sibling surfaces that already did; that makes the boolean meaningful for the page. A CDN hop remains a layer this flag cannot describe, and no in-repo mechanism detects it - recorded rather than claimed closed. THE GENERAL POINT, worth more than the fix: a freshness flag is only as truthful as the last cache between the code that sets it and the eye that reads it, and the timestamp survives where the boolean does not.
